title: Mathemyths: Leveraging Large Language Models to Teach Mathematical Language through Child-AI Co-Creative Storytelling
venue: Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '24)
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a large-language-model-based conversational agent can serve as an effective storytelling partner for young children learning mathematical language. The authors focus on early childhood math vocabulary development, arguing that children learn mathematical language well through guided storytelling with a knowledgeable partner, but that one-on-one human support is resource-intensive and difficult to scale. The study asks how prompt engineering can optimize an LLM for child-facing educational storytelling, whether children find such interactions engaging, and whether learning outcomes are comparable to those from human-child storytelling.

To address this, the authors developed Mathemyths, a GPT-4-powered voice-based co-creative storytelling system for children ages 4–8. The system alternates turns with children to build stories, asks open-ended questions, gives feedback, continues the narrative while embedding target math terms, and provides scaffolding when children are unsure or offer minimal responses. The target terms were six early math vocabulary words: sum, estimate, add, subtract, equal, and half. The paper also documents an iterative prompt-engineering and model-evaluation process comparing prompt-engineered GPT-4 outputs with human-generated content and a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 baseline.

The user study involved 35 children recruited from two public libraries in a midwestern U.S. city during summer 2023. Children were randomly assigned to co-create stories either with Mathemyths or with a trained human partner, completed pre- and post-tests of math language knowledge, and then provided enjoyment ratings. The storytelling activity lasted about 12 minutes total, with two short stories. Parents also completed demographic questionnaires. In addition to learning outcomes, the researchers analyzed engagement indicators such as response rates, response length, uncertainty, and story-creation performance.

The main finding is that children who interacted with Mathemyths showed significant improvement in mathematical language, and these gains were comparable overall to those of children working with a human partner. The AI condition showed a particular advantage on definition-related questions, while both younger and older children benefited, with older children showing somewhat stronger gains descriptively. Children were highly engaged with the AI, responding to most prompts, though human partners elicited somewhat longer and more substantial responses. Overall, the paper concludes that LLM-based storytelling agents can provide a viable and engaging educational experience for supporting early math language learning, while also highlighting differences in how children interact with AI versus human partners.

identified_tools.name: Mathemyths
identified_tools.description: A GPT-based voice conversational co-creative storytelling system for children ages 4–8 that alternates turns with a child to build stories while embedding and explaining mathematical vocabulary.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an AI storytelling partner for children to co-create two short stories and learn six mathematical terms (sum, estimate, add, subtract, equal, half), compared against a human storytelling partner.

findings.finding_summary: In a user study with 35 children ages 4–8, children showed significant improvement in total math language scores from pre-test (M=16.686, SD=9.578) to post-test (M=18.971, SD=1.526), F(1,31)=17.009, p<.000. Learning gains were comparable between the Mathemyths condition (pre: M=17.105, SD=9.882; post: M=19.500, SD=11.074; n=19) and the human condition (pre: M=16.187, SD=9.501; post: M=18.344, SD=10.158; n=16), with no condition difference, F(1,31)=0.012, p=.912.
findings.measure: 24-item math language assessment total score covering definition, recall, transfer, and practice of six target math terms

findings.finding_summary: Mathemyths showed a significant advantage for definition learning: children in the AI condition improved on definition questions from pre: M=2.737, SD=1.939 to post: M=3.368, SD=2.047, F(1,18)=8.308, p=.010. In contrast, children with a human partner did not significantly improve on definition items, F(1,15)=0.015, p=.903 (pre: M=2.813, SD=1.621; post: M=2.844, SD=1.777).
findings.measure: Definition subscale of the math language questionnaire

findings.finding_summary: Children actively engaged with Mathemyths, responding to over 95% of its questions, with responses averaging 6–10 words in length. However, children were generally more responsive and gave longer answers to a human partner, and Mathemyths elicited fewer substantial responses and more uncertain responses such as 'I don't know' (9.9% vs. 1.8% with a human).
findings.measure: Behavioral engagement indicators: response rate, response length, and coded response type during story co-creation

findings.finding_summary: Differences in engagement by age and partner type were descriptive but not statistically significant. Younger children behaved similarly with AI and human partners, while older children tended to give more frequent and longer responses to humans than to Mathemyths, but two-way ANOVA analyses found no significant age-group differences across engagement dimensions.
findings.measure: Age-stratified behavioral engagement comparisons during story co-creation

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical user study with random assignment to AI versus human partner, but the sample is small (n=35) and the design is closer to a lab-based comparative user study than a strong educational efficacy trial. Effect sizes and confidence intervals are not reported, limiting causal evidence strength.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports significant pre-post gains and comparable outcomes to a human partner, plus an advantage on definition items, but magnitude is unclear because no effect sizes are reported. Engagement results are mixed, so overall impact is promising but not yet clearly substantial.
